response_text: Yielding and time-based preemptive context switching can work together because they both ultimately trigger the same underlying context-switching mechanism through different paths - osYield() generates a software interrupt (SVC) that calls the scheduler, while the timer generates a hardware interrupt (SysTick) that also calls the scheduler, and both mechanisms converge on the same scheduler function that decides which thread should run next. The key is that both mechanisms are non-interfering: a thread can voluntarily yield before its time slice expires (cooperative behavior), or if it doesn't yield, the timer will eventually force a context switch (preemptive behavior), ensuring that the system maintains responsiveness regardless of thread behavior. This hybrid approach combines the efficiency of cooperative multitasking (threads can yield when they're naturally at good stopping points) with the reliability of preemptive multitasking (preventing any thread from monopolizing the CPU), creating a robust system where well-behaved threads can optimize their own context switches while poorly behaved threads are automatically managed by the timer-based preemption.\n
